pages.answer: Usually 6 to 8 times its rated current
pages.name: Starting a motor
options: About its rated current
Usually 6 to 8 times its rated current
About twice its rated current
pages.task: You start a motor direct on line. As it starts, about how much current does it draw?
pages.why: Usually 6 to 8 times, and sometimes more than 10 times. A soft starter cuts that. It brings the voltage up gently. Its switches are thyristors. Here is how they work.

pages.alt: A 230 V supply feeds a heater through one thyristor, drawn with its gate lead. It is off now. One cycle of the supply, 0° to 360°, drawn thin. The voltage across the load is drawn bold, and each slice that conducts is shaded. Gate pulses are marked at 90°.
pages.name: A diode with a gate
pages.text: A thyristor is a diode that also blocks forward voltage until a pulse on its gate fires it. Fired at 90°, it stays on after the pulse ends, until its current falls away near 180°. So the heater's voltage is shaded from 90° to 180° only. The negative half is empty. A second pulse at 135° changes nothing.

pages.alt: A 230 V supply feeds a heater through one thyristor, drawn with its gate lead. It is off now. One cycle of the supply, 0° to 360°, drawn thin. The voltage across the load is drawn bold, and each slice that conducts is shaded. Gate pulses are marked at 90°.
pages.answer: It conducts on until its current falls away, near 180°
pages.name: After the pulse
options: It turns off at once, as the pulse is over
It conducts on into the negative half
It conducts on until its current falls away, near 180°
pages.task: The thyristor fired at 90°, and the gate pulse is over. The cursor is at 120°. What happens next?
pages.why: It conducts on. Once fired, a thyristor latches on. The gate then has no more say. It lets go only when its current falls below a small holding current. On AC that happens just before the zero. So it needs a fresh pulse every cycle.

pages.alt: A 230 V supply feeds a heater through one thyristor, drawn with its gate lead. It is off now. One cycle of the supply, 0° to 360°, drawn thin. The voltage across the load is drawn bold, and each slice that conducts is shaded. Gate pulses are marked at 90°.
pages.name: The firing angle
pages.text: The firing angle, α, is the angle in each half where the gate fires. At 0°, the whole positive hump is shaded, and the average reads 104 V. At 90°, only its second half is shaded, and the average reads 52 V.

pages.alt: A 230 V supply feeds a heater through one thyristor, drawn with its gate lead. It is off now. One cycle of the supply, 0° to 360°, drawn thin. The voltage across the load is drawn bold, and each slice that conducts is shaded. Gate pulses are marked at 60°.
pages.name: Fire at 60°
options: About 78 V
About 69 V, a third less
About 52 V
pages.task: Fire at 60° instead. That cuts a third of the time from the positive half. What does the average become?
pages.why: About 78 V. The area under a sine from α to 180° is 1 + cos α. The whole hump gives 2. At 60° that is 1 + 0.5 = 1.5. That is three quarters of 2. So the average is 104 × 0.75, about 78 V. The start of a hump is low. So cutting it costs little.

pages.alt: A 230 V supply feeds a heater through four thyristors in a diamond, each drawn with its gate lead. No pair conducts now. One cycle of the supply, 0° to 360°, drawn thin. The voltage across the load is drawn bold, and each slice that conducts is shaded. Gate pulses are marked at 60° and 240°.
pages.name: A controlled bridge
pages.text: A bridge rectifier with thyristors in place of its four diodes is a controlled rectifier. Its average is (Vmax ÷ π)(1 + cos α). With α at 60°, both halves are shaded from 60° on, and the average reads 155 V.

pages.alt: A 230 V supply feeds a heater through four thyristors in a diamond, each drawn with its gate lead. No pair conducts now. One cycle of the supply, 0° to 360°, drawn thin. The voltage across the load is drawn bold, and each slice that conducts is shaded. Gate pulses are marked at 120° and 300°.
pages.name: Fire at 120°
options: About 69 V, a third of 207 V
About 52 V
About −52 V, as cos 120° is negative
pages.task: Now fire the bridge at 120°. What does it average?
pages.why: About 52 V. cos 120° is −0.5. So 1 + cos α is 0.5. That is a quarter of the whole hump's 2. A quarter of 207 V is about 52 V.

pages.alt: A 230 V supply feeds a heater through a triac, drawn with its gate lead. It is off now. One cycle of the supply, 0° to 360°, drawn thin. The voltage across the load is drawn bold, and each slice that conducts is shaded. Gate pulses are marked at 90° and 270°.
pages.name: The triac
pages.text: A triac behaves like two thyristors back to back, so it fires in both halves. With α at 90°, both halves are shaded from 90° on, one above the line and one below. The rms reads 163 V and the heater power 1150 W. The chopped current gives a power factor of about 0.71.

pages.alt: A 230 V supply feeds a heater through a triac, drawn with its gate lead. It is off now. One cycle of the supply, 0° to 360°, drawn thin. The voltage across the load is drawn bold, and each slice that conducts is shaded. Gate pulses are marked at 90° and 270°.
pages.answer: No, a lamp dimmer is for resistive loads only
pages.name: A fan on a dimmer
options: Yes, a lower rms means a slower fan
Yes, as the fan is small
No, a lamp dimmer is for resistive loads only
pages.task: A triac lamp dimmer is to hand. Should it set the speed of a small fan motor?
pages.why: No. Triac lamp dimmers are made for resistive loads only. They should not be used as a motor speed controller. A motor's coil keeps its current flowing past the voltage's zero. A heater's current falls to zero with the voltage. A soft starter or fan controller is built for a coil's late current. A lamp dimmer is not.

pages.alt: A 230 V supply feeds a battery through a choke through four thyristors in a diamond, each drawn with its gate lead. One pair conducts now. One cycle of the supply, 0° to 360°, drawn thin. The voltage across the load is drawn bold, and each slice that conducts is shaded. Gate pulses are marked at 30° and 210°. Below, the supply current is a block that starts 30° after the voltage.
pages.name: The charger
pages.text: A choke, a large coil, keeps the charger's current flowing, so each pair conducts from α to 180° + α. The slice's area is 2 cos α against a whole hump's 2, so the average is 207 × cos α. With α at 30°, it reads 179 V.

pages.alt: A 230 V supply feeds a battery through a choke through four thyristors in a diamond, each drawn with its gate lead. One pair conducts now. One cycle of the supply, 0° to 360°, drawn thin. The voltage across the load is drawn bold, and each slice that conducts is shaded. Gate pulses are marked at 30° and 210°. Below, the supply current is a block that starts 30° after the voltage.
pages.name: The power factor
pages.text: The supply's current is a block that starts α after the voltage. A block is not a sine, so even in step its power factor is only about 0.9. With α at 30°, the block starts 30° late, and the power factor reads 0.78, about 0.9 × cos α.

pages.alt: A 230 V supply feeds a battery through a choke through four thyristors in a diamond, each drawn with its gate lead. One pair conducts now. One cycle of the supply, 0° to 360°, drawn thin. The voltage across the load is drawn bold, and each slice that conducts is shaded. Gate pulses are marked at 60° and 240°. Below, the supply current is a block that starts 60° after the voltage.
pages.name: Half the output
options: It stays near 0.90, as firing later costs nothing
It falls to about 0.45
It rises, as less power is drawn
pages.task: The charger must cut its output to about 104 V, half of 207 V. What happens to its power factor?
pages.why: It falls to about 0.45. Half of 207 V needs cos α = 0.5. So α is 60°. The current block now starts 60° behind the voltage. A block scores only 0.9, even in step. So the power factor is 0.9 × 0.5 = 0.45. The supply carries the same current for half the power.

pages.alt: A 230 V supply feeds a heater through a triac, drawn with its gate lead. It is off now. One cycle of the supply, 0° to 360°, drawn thin. The voltage across the load is drawn bold, and each slice that conducts is shaded. Gate pulses are marked at 0° and 180°.
pages.answer: A voltage that ramps up from low to full
pages.name: The soft starter
options: A voltage that ramps up from low to full
The full voltage at once, for less time
A DC voltage that rises
pages.task: A soft starter fires its thyristors late at first, then earlier and earlier. What does the motor get?
pages.why: A ramp. Late firing passes only a thin slice of each half. So the motor sees a low voltage. Earlier firing widens the slices until the motor gets the full supply. That ramp limits the starting current.

pages.alt: A 230 V supply feeds a heater through four thyristors in a diamond, each drawn with its gate lead. No pair conducts now. One cycle of the supply, 0° to 360°, drawn thin. The voltage across the load is drawn bold, and each slice that conducts is shaded. Gate pulses are marked at 0° and 180°.
pages.answer: About 207 V, as if fired at 0°
pages.name: Gate stuck on
options: Nothing, as no fresh pulse ever comes
About 104 V, as before
About 207 V, as if fired at 0°
pages.task: A fault holds the gate signal on all the time. What does the heater get now?
pages.why: About 207 V. A thyristor fires once it is forward biased with its gate signalled. With the signal always on, each one fires at the start of its half. So the bridge acts as a plain diode bridge.
